headline: The Race at 3.8 Knots: Bass Working Valiant Rock, Slack Ticks In at 12:06
subhead: A tight thermal line from Kings Point to New London is stacking bait against the rips, and the bass know exactly where to sit.
body_markdown:
Three point eight knots. That's what the Race was doing on the max ebb Tuesday afternoon, and if you've fished this water for as long as I have, you know that number tells you almost everything before you even wet a line. Anything under three and the rips go soft, fish scatter, and you're marking bait instead of marking fish. Anything over four and you're fighting the current more than you're fishing it. Three point eight is the sweet spot — hard enough to hold bait against Valiant Rock and Race Rock, slow enough that a wire line with a bucktail can actually get down and stay down.

The slack window at Valiant Rock this week has been running short — call it ten, twelve minutes on either side of the turn, with the midday slack landing around 12:06 depending on the day. Miss that window and you're fighting green water the rest of the tide. I've had boats anchor up fifteen minutes too early and sit there watching their lines stream sideways, wondering why nothing's biting. There's nothing wrong with the fish. You're just not in the water yet.

The bite itself has been solid, not spectacular. Wire line trolled with bunker spoons and umbrella rigs off Race Rock has produced stripers in the 28 to 38-inch range on the last two hours of the ebb, with the occasional better fish pushing 20 pounds coming off the north side of Valiant where the rock drops into 40 feet. Bucktails — 3 to 4-ounce, white or chartreuse, tipped with a strip of mackerel — have been the better call on the drift through Plum Gut itself, worked slow along bottom as the current funnels bait through that gut like water through a fire hose. The fish are there, but you have to be patient with the retrieve. Too fast and you're pulling the jig out of the strike zone before a fish can commit.

Here's the why behind it. New London's reading around 67.5 degrees right now, a good three and a half degrees cooler than Kings Point at 71.2. That gradient is exactly what's staging fish along the eastern Sound rips — the cooler, oxygen-rich water holds bait tighter, and the bass know it. They're not spread out chasing forage across open water; they're pinned against structure where the current concentrates everything for them. That's Valiant Rock. That's Race Rock. That's the north edge of the Sluiceway where the bottom breaks hard and the tide rips through Little Gull and Great Gull.

Fluke fishing off the Sluiceway has been mixed — some days you limit out on keepers in the 18 to 22-inch range drifting Gulp swimming mullets in white over 25 to 35 feet of sandy bottom, other days you grind through a dozen shorts before you find a keeper. The water's holding up fine, it's more about hitting the right stage of tide — the last hour of the incoming has been the most consistent, when the bait gets pushed up onto the flats between Great Gull and the Sluiceway proper.

Black sea bass around Valiant Rock and the rockpile structure off Race Rock have been dependable filler when the stripers go quiet, squid strips or clam on a two-hook bottom rig dropped right into the rock edges in 35 to 50 feet. Nothing huge, but steady action, and a good way to fill a cooler while you wait out a slack window.

Bluefish have been mixed into the Gut on the same tides as the bass, chopping up bucktails and forcing a lot of guys to switch to wire leader mid-drift. Not complaining — a 12-pound bluefish on light tackle in that current is its own kind of fun, even if it costs you a jig.

No albies yet, and I wouldn't expect them for another few weeks. The Gut usually doesn't see the first real push of false albacore until late August into September around here, once the water further offshore warms and the bait balls tighten up. There's chatter about squid concentrations building off Rhode Island and into Nantucket Sound as that water pushes past the high 50s and into the 60s — if that pattern holds and pushes west along the Race, it could supercharge things earlier than usual. I've seen that happen before, and when the squid show early, the striper bite at Valiant Rock gets downright violent for a stretch. Doesn't mean it's a lock, but it's exactly the kind of signal that makes me start rigging extra squid-strip bucktails just in case.

Looking ahead, if the current stays in that 3.5 to 4-knot range through the week and the thermal line holds where it is, I'd keep working the last two hours of ebb at Race Rock with wire line, and hit Valiant Rock right on that tight slack window with bucktails before the current builds back. If we get a stretch of southwest wind that muddies up the Gut, I'd shift effort to the Sluiceway fluke grounds where the bottom stays cleaner longer. Either way, know your slack to the minute before you leave the dock — out here, that's the difference between a good trip and a long ride home.
